phonemes.desc: Rough breathing on upsilon with acute [hý] — the name begins with a breathy, high-pitched syllable.
Delta-rho-alpha; the root ὕδωρ, 'water,' is visible, though the creature is a water-serpent in form and habitat.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HOO-drah' — the first syllable is pitched high and begins with a rough 'h'; the final -a is short.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: Ὕδρα (Hýdra), the water-serpent slain by Herakles

kin.label: Root
kin.form: ὕδωρ (hýdōr), 'water'; the Hydra is the dangerous aspect of stagnant water

pronunciation.note: Hýdra is Tier 2 because the Greek Ὕδρα preserves the acute stress on the first syllable but has no long vowel. The rough breathing on the upsilon is essential to the name's sound and identity.

domains.title: The Many-Headed Serpent
domains.subtitle: Regeneration, Stagnant Water, Heroic Trial
domains.lead: Hýdra is the monstrous water-serpent of Lerna, whose heads grew back when cut off. For Herakles, killing it required more than strength; it required fire, teamwork, and the recognition that some evils multiply when opposed directly.

cards.name: Regenerating Heads
cards.desc: Cut off one head and two grew back; the monster embodied the paradox of unending struggle.

cards.name: The Lerna Swamp
cards.desc: A marshy, stagnant region near Argos; the Hydra personifies corrupted water and hidden disease.

cards.name: Herakles' Second Labor
cards.desc: The greatest of Greek heroes defeated the Hydra with torch and club, aided by Iolaos.

cards.name: Immortal Head
cards.desc: One head could not be killed; Herakles buried it beneath a rock, still hissing.

symbols.name: Serpent heads
symbols.meaning: Multiplicity, regeneration, and the seemingly endless forms of evil

symbols.name: Torch
symbols.meaning: The fire used by Iolaos to cauterize the stumps and prevent regrowth

symbols.name: Lerna swamp
symbols.meaning: Stagnant water as the breeding ground of plague and monster

symbols.name: Crab
symbols.meaning: The crab sent by Hera to harass Herakles during the combat

mythology.lead: Hýdra's myth is a labor of escalation. Herakles must discover that brute force alone feeds the monster; victory comes only when fire meets flesh at the exact moment of severance.

myths.title: The Brood of Typhon and Echidna
myths.text: Hesiod gives the Hydra a monstrous pedigree. She is the child of Typhon and Echidna — the storm-fiend and the she-viper — and thus the sister of Cerberus and the Chimaera, 'whom the white-crested Hera reared' against Herakles (Theogony 313–318, 333–335). Her home was the marsh of Lerna, beside the Alcyonian lake, a water so deep and foul that antiquity said its bottom had never been seen; Pausanias (2.36–37) records the ground's ill repute and the sanctuary of the Lernaean Demeter beside it. The genealogy is the myth's point: the Hydra is not a freak but a family — bred from the union of storm and serpent, fostered by a goddess with a grudge, and set down in stagnant water where sickness gathers. Before Herakles ever raises his club, the monster is already a theological statement: some evils are raised deliberately, in the dark, by powers that mean to test a hero.

myths.title: The Second Labor
myths.text: Eurystheus, king of Tiryns, sent Herakles against the Hydra as his second labor — a commission made hopeless by its own terms, for the beast had nine heads, or fifty, or a hundred, depending on the teller, and one of them was immortal. Heracles began as heroes begin: he lured the serpent from its lair with arrows, closed, and smashed the heads with his club (Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.2). For every head that fell, two grew back. Hera, the monster's foster-mother, sent a crab to fasten on Herakles' foot — the sidelong nip of panic at a hero's heel, immortalized in the constellation Cancer. The labor undoes the hero's entire method: where force had always answered, force now feeds the enemy. Apollodorus adds the bitter footnote that Eurystheus later refused to count the labor, precisely because Herakles accepted help. The myth's lesson arrives early: some trials are designed so that strength alone disqualifies you.

myths.title: Iolaos and the Fire
myths.text: The turn comes from outside the hero. Iolaos, Herakles' nephew and charioteer, saw what strength could not see: that each wound had to be burned shut the instant it was made. He brought fire, and as Herakles struck off each head, Iolaos cauterized the neck with a burning brand; the severed heads could no longer multiply (Apollodorus 2.5.2). In the fuller iconographic tradition Athena stands by as divine adviser — on scores of archaic vases the goddess directs the fire while the two men work. The immortal head Herakles cut off last and buried beneath a great rock on the road from Lerna to Elaious, where Apollodorus says it lay still breathing its poison. The episode is the Greek hymn to technique over force: fire, timing and partnership defeat what the club could not. But the victory has a price the hero must accept — the labor must be shared, and so must the credit, or the hero dies.

myths.title: The Arrows of Gall
myths.text: Herakles then did the thing that would unmake him. He cut open the Hydra's body and steeped his arrows in its gall, making of each shaft a sure death (Apollodorus 2.5.2, 2.7.7). Years later the centaur Nessos, dying by one of those arrows, told Deianeira to keep his blood — now poisoned by the Hydra — as a love-charm; smeared on Herakles' robe, it consumed the hero on his own pyre (Sophocles, Women of Trachis 555–581). The bow passed to Philoctetes, whose festering wound the Greeks could not heal, and it was one of these arrows that killed Paris and broke the siege of Troy (Apollodorus, Epitome). The myth follows the poison across a whole career: the weapon that won the labor became the agent of the hero's death, the army's curse, and the war's end. The Greeks kept the receipt — triumph always carries its toxin forward. The hydra's real head was never buried: it was dipped, and it traveled.

lore.syncretism: The Hydra has no independent cult but belongs to a broader Greek and Near Eastern tradition of multi-headed water serpents defeated by storm-gods or heroes. The Lernaean Hydra influenced later dragon lore, including medieval accounts of regenerating dragons. In modern biology, 'hydra' names a genus of freshwater cnidarian capable of remarkable regeneration — a scientific tribute to the myth. The constellation Hydra preserves the serpent in the southern sky.
lore.culturalLegacy: 'Hydra-headed' has become an idiom for any problem that grows worse when attacked. The monster appears in comic books, films, and political metaphors as the image of resilient, multiplying evil. Its scientific namesake, the hydra, makes the myth literal: a tiny animal that regenerates from fragments, immortal in its own small way.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hýdra is the lesson that some enemies cannot be defeated by the same energy that animates them. Cut a head and the body grows stronger; meet rage with rage and the conflict feeds itself. The myth recommends precision, partnership, and the right tool at the right moment.

Yet there is also humility in the labor. Herakles needs help. The greatest hero cannot do it alone. And one head remains unkillable, buried rather than destroyed — a reminder that some dangers are managed, not solved. The Hydra teaches both strategy and acceptance: fight with fire, but know that the immortal head still breathes beneath the stone.
lore.archaeology: The Lerna region in the Argolid preserves Bronze Age remains and a late mythic association with the Hydra. The combat was a favorite subject in Greek vase painting from the Archaic period onward, showing Herakles and Iolaos attacking the multi-headed serpent, often with Athena directing the fire. The constellation Hydra was catalogued by Ptolemy and transmitted through medieval and Renaissance star atlases.
